extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in research integrity: journal editors, researchers, watchdogs, and the scientifically literate public
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating the integrity and trustworthiness of a published clinical trial paper and the journal's handling of concerns (data, authorship, registration, COI, and retraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data irregularities / inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal found 'apparent recruitment outside of the inclusion criteria, including those over 65 years old; discrepancy in the number of participants enrolled; and data irregularities, such as unusual patterns in the data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat recruitment outside inclusion criteria, participant-count discrepancies, and unusual data patterns as substantive reasons to question a paper's trustworthiness and to investigate or retract. Examples given: 'discrepancy in the number of participants enrolled' and 'unusual patterns in the data.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific data-pattern red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers noted a 'curious repeating pattern' of records in the dataset and a high number of integers for the height and weight of patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repeating records, suspiciously rounded or integer-valued biometrics, and other statistical anomalies as potential signs of error or fabrication; these are actionable red flags for reviewers and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sharing and open-data availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers were able to identify some of the data concerns because the data 'were made publicly available in an open access repository in line with The BMJ’s data-sharing policy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making datasets publicly available enables post-publication scrutiny. However, availability alone is not sufficient — journals should consider reviewing datasets before publication as well ('the data were not reviewed by the journal before publication').

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal review of underlying data prior to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice states 'the data were not reviewed by the journal before publication' and that 'the journal is currently trialling how it might better manage review of data before publication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should implement procedures to assess submitted datasets during peer review or editorial checks to catch inconsistencies before publication; trialling formal data-review workflows is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset availability during peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the data issues 'could have been flagged during peer review, but the sequence of events ... suggests the authors didn’t share the dataset until after the manuscript had already been reviewed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that authors provide underlying data (or sufficient summaries) to peer reviewers at the time of review so reviewers can assess data integrity and spot anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospective trial registration / timing of registration
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notice flagged 'inconsistent information about the timing of recruitment and the registration of the study.' It also states: 'The BMJ does not publish retrospectively registered trials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trials should be registered prospectively (before patient enrollment); inconsistent or retrospectively amended registration dates are grounds for concern and can render a trial ineligible for publication in journals that forbid retrospective registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship transparency, contribution, and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Two named cardiologists were removed as authors; the notice says they 'provided “feedback on the manuscript before its submission.”' They asked to be removed prior to publication and did not respond to subsequent emails during submission; authors asked the journal to be removed after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorship should reflect substantive contributions and responsibility. All named authors should engage with the submission process, respond to journal queries, and confirm authorship; late removals or noncommunication are red flags requiring clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest disclosure and management
rubrics_metrics.description: PubPeer sleuths pointed out potential conflicts of interest: one author 'is a director of the Heart Cells Company' and 'a trustee' of a foundation that funds a unit led by him that administers stem cell therapies to patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts of interest must be disclosed and managed. While COI is common and not by itself proof of misconduct, undeclared or unmanaged COI may warrant deeper scrutiny of study conduct and data integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and consistent reporting of protocol and study documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors' submitted protocol indicated the trial was registered before patient enrollment, but a previous publication of the protocol and clinicaltrials.gov original date indicated registration after recruitment began; the date was later amended 'in a way which suggested that the study had been registered prospectively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication materials (protocols, registry entries, prior publications) must be internally consistent and transparently dated; post hoc amendments that make registration appear prospective are unacceptable and justify investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt journal investigation and corrective action when patient safety is implicated
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that The BMJ 'did not retract the article more swiftly, given the implications for patient safety' and criticism that the journal 'seemed more interested in seeking an external opinion rather than relying on their own independent experts, thereby delaying retraction and putting patient safety at risk.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When data or conduct issues have potential patient-safety implications, journals should prioritize timely internal assessment and corrective actions (expressions of concern, retractions) instead of delays that could put patients at risk; liaising with regulators is appropriate but should not unreasonably delay action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of external regulators and investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ 'had asked the Iran Food and Drug Administration to assess concerns about the paper, but stopped receiving responses from the organization in December.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may seek regulator investigations for trials, but should have contingency plans if regulators are unresponsive and should continue independent assessment to avoid indefinite delay in remedial actions.
